findings.source_passage: their captain snapped his fingers in the plaintiffs' teeth, and assured them that by way of doxology to the deed he had done, he would now retain their line
findings.source_locator: paragraph describing the whale-trover case, after 'very eyes of the plaintiffs'
findings.why_it_matters: The captain's contemptuous gesture and the word 'doxology' are signature Melvillean irony and voice; the draft simply says the defendants retained the gear without this vivid, rhetorically distinct detail.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'snapped his fingers in the plaintiffs' teeth' sentence and the 'doxology' phrase verbatim; they are compact enough to include without budget damage.

findings.source_passage: Now in the present case Erskine contended that the examples of the whale and the lady were reciprocally illustrative of each other.
findings.source_locator: paragraph immediately after the crim. con. analogy
findings.why_it_matters: This deadpan sentence is the comic capstone of the crim. con. digression; its dry legalistic voice is distinctively Melvillean and the draft omits it entirely, losing the rhetorical punch.
findings.suggested_fix: Add the sentence verbatim after the Erskine/lady account.

findings.source_passage: A common man looking at this decision of the very learned Judge, might possibly object to it.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'A common man looking at this decision'
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence sets up the ironic pivot from dry legal commentary to sweeping philosophical/political application; its absence makes the transition to 'fundamentals of all human jurisprudence' feel abrupt and strips the irony of the legal satire.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'A common man…might possibly object' sentence before the 'ploughed to the primary rock' passage.

summary: The draft faithfully preserves the chapter's most famous passages (the two laws, the Fast-Fish rhetorical cascade, the closing 'reader' address, and the Temple of the Philistines metaphor) but loses three mid-chapter voice moments—the captain's contemptuous 'doxology' gesture, Erskine's reciprocal-illustration summary, and the 'common man might object' pivot—that carry significant ironic and rhetorical weight; none rises to high severity, but the three medium findings together approach the regenerate threshold.
